name: Aceh
description: Situated at the northern tip of Sumatra, Aceh is known as Serambi Mekkah (Veranda of Mecca) for its deep Islamic heritage and resilient history. Its capital, Banda Aceh, anchors a coastline framed by the Baiturrahman Grand Mosque, Tsunami Museum, and the coral reefs of Sabang on Weh Island. Inland, the Leuser Ecosystem shelters Sumatran orangutans and tigers, while the Gayo Highlands produce prized single-origin Arabica coffee alongside rich culinary staples such as Mie Aceh and Ayam Tangkap.

name: Sumatera Utara
description: Sumatera Utara stretches from the Strait of Malacca across the volcanic Bukit Barisan mountains to the Indian Ocean, centered around the bustling metropolis of Medan. The province is home to Lake Toba, the world’s largest volcanic caldera lake, and cultural Samosir Island, heartland of Batak heritage, traditional ulos weaving, and stone-carved villages. Visitors also explore Gunung Leuser National Park’s rainforests, Sipiso-piso Waterfall, and Medan’s renowned culinary scene featuring Bika Ambon and Soto Medan.

name: Sumatera Barat
description: Set along western Sumatra’s dramatic coast and highland valleys, Sumatera Barat is the ancestral homeland of the matrilineal Minangkabau people, governed from Padang. Iconic curved-roof Rumah Gadang architecture dots scenic Bukittinggi, Sianok Canyon, and the turquoise volcanic lakes of Maninjau and Singkarak, while the Mentawai Islands attract surfers worldwide. Globally celebrated for Padang cuisine—especially Rendang, Sate Padang, and Dendeng Balado—the province blends spice-rich culinary craft with living adat traditions and vibrant coastal landscapes.

name: Riau
description: Lying along Sumatra’s central eastern lowlands and major river arteries such as the Siak and Kampar, Riau serves as an energy, palm-oil, and Malay cultural hub centered in Pekanbaru. Historic landmarks include the Muara Takus Buddhist temple complex, Siak Sri Indrapura Palace, and traditional Malay poetry and zapin dance traditions. Along the Kampar River, the famous Bono tidal bore creates miles-long river waves, while coastal estuaries and peatland parks sustain rich riverine fisheries and wildlife.

name: Kepulauan Riau
description: Spanning more than 2,400 islands across the South China Sea and Malacca Strait gateways, Kepulauan Riau is governed from historic Tanjung Pinang on Bintan Island. Its archipelago merges maritime trade corridors and Batam’s industrial ports with serene white-sand resorts, Penyengat Island’s royal Malay heritage, and granite-boulder beaches in Natuna and Anambas. Fresh seafood dishes like Gonggong sea snails and Mie Lendir reflect a lively seafaring culture linking Sumatra, Singapore, and Borneo.

name: Jambi
description: Bisected by Sumatra’s longest river, the Batanghari, Jambi extends from eastern peat coasts to the towering volcanic peaks of Kerinci Seblat National Park around its capital, Jambi City. The province safeguards the sprawling Muaro Jambi temple compound—one of Southeast Asia’s largest ancient brick Buddhist sites—alongside Mount Kerinci, Indonesia’s highest active volcano. Rich tea plantations, Lake Gunung Tujuh, and traditional Tempoyak fermented durian dishes highlight Jambi’s blend of highland wilderness and river heritage.

name: Sumatera Selatan
description: Anchored by Palembang along the wide Musi River, Sumatera Selatan inherits the maritime legacy of the ancient Srivijaya Empire, symbolized by the towering Ampera Bridge and Kemaro Island. Beyond its riverfront markets and Musi delta trade, the province encompasses fertile highland coffee estates around Pagar Alam and Mount Dempo’s volcanic slopes. Palembang’s culinary fame centers on Pempek savory fishcakes served with tangy cuko sauce, songket gold-threaded textiles, and lively river festivals.

name: Kepulauan Bangka Belitung
description: Located off southeastern Sumatra across the Karimata Strait, Kepulauan Bangka Belitung consists of twin main islands and hundreds of smaller islets administered from Pangkal Pinang. Belitung’s Tanjung Tinggi Beach is famous for towering granite boulders framing crystal-clear turquoise coves, while Bangka’s coastline offers lighthouse islands and historic tin-mining towns. Famous for white pepper plantations, coastal seafood such as Mie Bangka and Lempah Kuning, and serene island-hopping routes, the province blends geological drama with relaxed island life.

name: Bengkulu
description: Facing the open Indian Ocean along Sumatra’s southwestern coast, Bengkulu blends lush Bukit Barisan rainforests with rare colonial heritage centered in Bengkulu City. The province preserves Fort Marlborough—an 18th-century British fortress—alongside the historic residence where Sukarno lived during exile, and is famous as a natural habitat for the giant Rafflesia arnoldii bloom. Coastal beaches like Pantai Panjang, highland tea hills in Kepahiang, and traditional Tabot ceremonies define its distinctive cultural rhythm.

name: Lampung
description: Occupying Sumatra’s southern tip overlooking the Sunda Strait, Lampung connects Sumatra and Java through major ferry ports while centering administration in Bandar Lampung. Way Kambas National Park protects wild Sumatran elephants and rhinos, while Kiluan Bay draws visitors for dolphin watching and Krakatau volcano rises nearby in the strait. Known for intricate Tapis gold-embroidered woven cloth, strong Robusta coffee, and Seruit fish dishes, Lampung showcases both coastal vistas and fertile agricultural highlands.

name: DKI Jakarta
description: As Indonesia’s historic maritime capital and commercial nerve center on Java’s northwest coast, DKI Jakarta weaves centuries of Betawi, Dutch colonial, and modern cosmopolitan life into a dynamic megacity. Iconic landmarks range from the towering National Monument (Monas) and Istiqlal Mosque to Kota Tua’s heritage squares, Sunda Kelapa harbor, and the coral islets of Kepulauan Seribu. Dynamic arts districts, sprawling malls, and iconic dishes such as Kerak Telor and Soto Betawi capture the city’s fast-paced energy.

name: Jawa Barat
description: Ringed by misty volcanic highlands and tea plantations, Jawa Barat is Indonesia’s most populous province and the cultural heartland of the Sundanese people, governed from Bandung. Its cool plateaus showcase Tangkuban Perahu crater, Kawah Putih’s sulfur lake, Pangandaran’s coastal reserves, and Bogor’s historic Botanical Gardens. Celebrated for Sundanese angklung bamboo music, vibrant creative industries, and fresh specialties such as Nasi Timbel, Batagor, and Peuyeum, the province balances highland beauty with bustling urban innovation.

name: Banten
description: Occupying Java’s westernmost peninsula along the Sunda Strait, Banten pairs thriving industrial corridors around Serang and Tangerang with wild coastlines and living indigenous heritage. Ujung Kulon National Park—a UNESCO World Heritage site—protects the last wild Javan rhinoceroses, while Old Banten’s Great Mosque and royal ruins recall a powerful 16th-century Islamic sultanate. Visitors also explore Sawarna’s surf beaches, Tanjung Lesung, and the secluded Baduy highland communities known for centuries-old ecological traditions.

name: Jawa Tengah
description: Located in the cultural core of Java and administered from coastal Semarang, Jawa Tengah preserves monumental temple architecture, Javanese court arts, and dramatic volcanic landscapes. The province houses Borobudur, the world’s largest Buddhist monument, alongside the towering Dieng Plateau temples, Karimunjawa’s marine archipelago, and Semarang’s Dutch heritage district of Kota Lama. Deeply rooted in batik craftsmanship, wayang shadow puppetry, and gamelan music, its culinary classics include Lumpia Semarang, Gudeg-influenced stews, and Soto Kudus.

name: DI Yogyakarta
description: A special autonomous region led by a reigning Sultan in Yogyakarta, DI Yogyakarta serves as Java’s preeminent center of classical court culture, education, and fine arts. Iconic treasures include the royal Kraton palace, Prambanan’s soaring Hindu spires, Malioboro’s bustling craft promenade, and the volcanic cone of Mount Merapi to the north. From hand-drawn batik and silverwork in Kotagede to black-sand southern beaches and sweet-savory Gudeg jackfruit stew, the province radiates timeless Javanese elegance.

name: Jawa Timur
description: Spanning eastern Java and Madura Island from its port capital of Surabaya, Jawa Timur boasts some of Indonesia’s most dramatic volcanic scenery and ancient Majapahit heritage. Sunrise views over Mount Bromo’s sea of sand, the electric-blue sulfur flames of Kawah Ijen, and lush waterfalls such as Tumpak Sewu draw travelers year-round. Known for Surabaya’s heroic history, Madurese bull races, bold East Javanese dishes like Rawon and Rujak Cingur, and vibrant coastal trade, it blends rugged nature with industrial strength.

name: Bali
description: Known worldwide as the Island of the Gods, Bali pairs vibrant Hindu-Balinese spirituality with terraced emerald landscapes and coastal cliffs surrounding its capital, Denpasar. UNESCO-listed Subak rice terraces in Jatiluwih, cliffside Uluwatu Temple, Lake Bratan’s water shrines, and Ubud’s dance and painting studios embody living ceremonial life. From world-class surf breaks and Nusa Penida’s limestone coves to aromatic Babi Guling, Lawar, and gamelan ensembles, Bali offers unmatched cultural depth and natural charm.

name: Nusa Tenggara Barat
description: Stretching across Lombok and Sumbawa islands east of Bali, Nusa Tenggara Barat blends Sasak and Samawa traditions around its capital, Mataram. Towering Mount Rinjani shelters the volcanic Lake Segara Anak, while the car-free Gili Islands, Kuta Mandalika’s sweeping bays, and Sumbawa’s Moyo Island offer pristine coral reefs and world-class surf. Hand-woven songket textiles, spicy Ayam Taliwang and Plecing Kangkung, and wild horse pastures in Sumbawa give the province an adventurous, uncrowded character.

name: Nusa Tenggara Timur
description: Encompassing more than 500 rugged islands across eastern Indonesia—including Flores, Sumba, and West Timor—Nusa Tenggara Timur is governed from Kupang. The province protects the legendary Komodo dragons of Komodo National Park, the tri-colored volcanic crater lakes of Kelimutu, Padar Island’s ridges, and traditional megalithic villages in Sumba. Renowned for intricate hand-dyed ikat weaving, savannas studded with lontar palms, and crystal-clear diving waters in Alor and Labuan Bajo, NTT offers dramatic frontier beauty.

name: Kalimantan Barat
description: Straddling the equator along Borneo’s western coast and governed from Pontianak, Kalimantan Barat is shaped by the mighty Kapuas—Indonesia’s longest river—and sweeping tropical rainforests. Pontianak’s Equator Monument marks zero degrees latitude, while inland lakes in Danau Sentarum National Park and Betung Kerihun safeguard rare orangutan habitats and Dayak longhouses. Rich Chinese-Indonesian, Malay, and Dayak traditions shine through Singkawang’s Cap Go Meh festival, woven rattan crafts, and riverfront culinary specialties.

name: Kalimantan Tengah
description: Covering vast peat-swamp forests and winding blackwater rivers in southern Borneo, Kalimantan Tengah is centered in the spacious, tree-lined capital of Palangka Raya. Tanjung Puting National Park is famous worldwide for klotok riverboat journeys through wild orangutan, proboscis monkey, and hornbill sanctuaries, alongside Sebangau’s peatland biodiversity. Deeply anchored in Dayak Ngaju philosophy, sacred Sandung memorials, and river-focused livelihoods, the province highlights the vital ecological wealth of Borneo’s rainforest heartland.

name: Kalimantan Selatan
description: Situated at Borneo’s southeastern corner and administered from Banjarbaru alongside historic port city Banjarmasin, Kalimantan Selatan is famed as the "Land of a Thousand Rivers." Dawn boat traders still gather at Lok Baintan’s vibrant floating markets, while the Meratus Mountains offer bamboo rafting, waterfalls, and indigenous Dayak Meratus villages. Known for Martapura’s diamond-polishing markets, shimmering Sasirangan tie-dyed cloth, and hearty Soto Banjar soup, the province blends river commerce with highland adventure.

name: Kalimantan Timur
description: Stretching along Borneo’s eastern coast from Samarinda and port hub Balikpapan, Kalimantan Timur combines rich energy resources with extraordinary rainforest and marine sanctuaries—and hosts the site of Indonesia’s future capital, Nusantara. Offshore, the Derawan Archipelago and Maratua Island shelter green sea turtles, stingless jellyfish lakes on Kakaban, and vibrant coral walls, while Kutai and Mahakam wetlands harbor rare freshwater Irrawaddy dolphins. Traditional Dayak Kenyah woodcarvings and riverine cuisine enrich this dynamic province.

name: Kalimantan Utara
description: Indonesia’s youngest province in Borneo, Kalimantan Utara borders Sabah and Sarawak along rugged forested highlands and coastal deltas, with Tanjung Selor as its capital. Kayan Mentarang National Park preserves one of Southeast Asia’s largest unbroken tracts of tropical rainforest and Dayak heritage, while Tarakan Island serves as an offshore gateway known for mangrove conservation and proboscis monkeys. Swiftlet caves, mountain rapids, and cross-border river trade give this northern frontier a quiet, untouched character.

name: Sulawesi Utara
description: Crowning Sulawesi’s northern peninsula around coastal Manado, Sulawesi Utara is famous for dramatic volcanoes, coral walls, and warm Minahasan hospitality. Bunaken National Marine Park offers world-renowned vertical reef diving, while the Minahasa Highlands frame Lake Tondano, Mount Lokon, and colorful traditional markets in Tomohon. Known for fiery spicy cuisine like Tinutuan porridge and Rica-Rica, lively kolintang xylophone ensembles, and endemic tarsiers in Tangkoko Nature Reserve, the province pairs marine splendor with highland charm.

name: Gorontalo
description: Nestled along Sulawesi’s northern arm between Tomini Bay and the Celebes Sea, Gorontalo offers serene coastal waters, rolling hills, and centuries-old Islamic-kingdom heritage around Gorontalo City. The historic Otanaha Fortress overlooks Lake Limboto, while Botubarani’s clear bay attracts whale sharks close to shore and Olele Marine Park showcases rare Salvador Dali coral sponges. Famous for sweet corn-based Binthe Biluhuta soup and Karawo hand-embroidered textiles, Gorontalo remains an inviting, tranquil northern gem.

name: Sulawesi Tengah
description: Forming the rugged central hub of Sulawesi around the deep bay city of Palu, Sulawesi Tengah spans mountain valleys, pristine reef archipelagos, and enigmatic ancient history. Lore Lindu National Park safeguards giant prehistoric stone megaliths in the Bada Valley alongside rare endemic birds, while the Togean Islands in Tomini Bay offer untouched lagoon diving and Bajau stilt villages. Known for Banggai’s limestone bays, Lake Poso, and traditional Kaledo beef-bone soup, the province rewards explorers with striking diversity.

name: Sulawesi Barat
description: Facing the Makassar Strait along western Sulawesi’s scenic coastline, Sulawesi Barat is governed from the seaside town of Mamuju and celebrated for proud Mandar maritime heritage. Traditional double-outrigger Sandeq sailboats—among the fastest wind-powered vessels in the archipelago—still race across coastal waters, while Mamasa’s misty highlands preserve carved wooden houses and terraced rice valleys. Rich in cocoa farms, silk weaving, and freshly grilled coastal fish with Jepa cassava flatbread, the province exudes authentic coastal warmth.

name: Sulawesi Selatan
description: Anchored by the historic maritime metropolis of Makassar, Sulawesi Selatan unites Bugis, Makassar, and Torajan cultures across fertile plains, limestone karst canyons, and dramatic highlands. In Tana Toraja, soaring boat-shaped Tongkonan roofs and cliffside burial terraces draw global admiration, while Rammang-Rammang’s karst towers, Fort Rotterdam, and white-sand Bira Beach showcase stunning natural and colonial landmarks. Iconic Phinisi wooden schooners, spicy Coto Makassar, and Pisang Epe reflect centuries of proud seafaring tradition.

name: Sulawesi Tenggara
description: Wrapping around Sulawesi’s southeastern peninsula and offshore islands from its capital, Kendari, Sulawesi Tenggara is a premier marine sanctuary and cultural crossroads. Wakatobi National Park—celebrated globally by divers—protects dazzling coral biodiversity and Bajau sea-nomad villages, while Buton Island’s massive Wolio Fortress and Labengki’s karst lagoons captivate visitors. Blessed with lush waterfalls, nickel-rich hills, and traditional cassava Sinonggi dishes, the province showcases some of Indonesia’s finest underwater and island scenery.

name: Maluku
description: Centered around Ambon in the legendary Spice Islands of eastern Indonesia, Maluku holds a storied place in world maritime history as the original home of nutmeg and cloves. Today, crystal-clear bays in the Banda Islands, Ora Beach’s dramatic Seram Island cliffs, and Kei Islands’ powdery white sands sit beside historic forts such as Belgica and Nieuw Victoria. Revered as a "City of Music," Ambon inspires harmonious vocal choirs, energetic Cakalele dances, and Papeda sago served with tangy yellow fish broth.

name: Maluku Utara
description: Comprising volcanic spice islands led by Halmahera, Ternate, and Tidore around the capital Sofifi on Halmahera’s coast, Maluku Utara blends towering island cones with royal sultanate history. Ternate’s Mount Gamalama and Tolukko Fort overlook the twin peak of Tidore across deep blue channels, while Morotai Island preserves WWII heritage alongside crystal diving lagoons. Rich in clove and nutmeg groves, Cendrawasih birdwatching in Halmahera’s forests, and spice-infused seafood, the province radiates historical intrigue.

name: Papua
description: Situated on New Guinea’s northern coast around scenic Jayapura and Humboldt Bay, Papua unites coastal cities, lush Cyclops Mountain rainforests, and vibrant Melanesian heritage. Lake Sentani—dotted with stilt villages, bark paintings, and annual cultural festivals—lies just inland from Jayapura’s turquoise beaches and Yotefa Bay bridges. Home to endemic birds-of-paradise, traditional noken woven bags, and sago-based cuisine like Papeda and grilled fish, Papua offers an inspiring gateway to Indonesia’s easternmost landscapes.

name: Papua Barat
description: Occupying the scenic Bird’s Head and Bomberai peninsulas around the coastal capital of Manokwari, Papua Barat blends misty Arfak Mountain birdwatching reserves with dramatic marine wilderness. Cenderawasih Bay National Park is celebrated worldwide for year-round encounters with gentle whale sharks near Kwatisore, while Mansinam Island marks a pivotal site in Papua’s modern spiritual history. Dense coastal mangroves, Triton Bay’s limestone bays, and warm Papuan hospitality highlight the province’s remarkable ecological richness.

name: Papua Selatan
description: Stretching across vast southern wetlands, savannas, and winding rivers toward Indonesia’s eastern border, Papua Selatan is anchored by the historic frontier city of Merauke. Wasur National Park—often called the Serengeti of Papua—protects sweeping marshlands, towering termite mounds, wallabies, and flocks of migratory birds, while Asmat communities along the coast are world-famous for intricate woodcarving artistry. Known for Indonesia’s easternmost zero-kilometer monument in Sota and abundant river fisheries, the province showcases expansive wilderness.

name: Papua Tengah
description: Extending from the coral-fringed shores of Cenderawasih Bay near its capital, Nabire, up to the towering glaciated peaks of the Sudirman Range, Papua Tengah showcases extraordinary elevation contrasts. Nabire’s clear waters shelter gentle whale sharks and coral reefs, while inland highlands hold Puncak Jaya (Carstensz Pyramid)—the highest mountain in Indonesia and Oceania—surrounded by Lorentz National Park’s alpine valleys. Traditional highland horticulture, coastal sago dishes, and distinct tribal heritage define this diverse region.

name: Papua Pegunungan
description: As Indonesia’s only landlocked province, Papua Pegunungan rises high in the central mountain spine of New Guinea, centered on Wamena in the lush Baliem Valley. Surrounded by emerald peaks, cool highland mist, and winding mountain rivers, the Baliem Valley preserves ancient Dani farming terraces, suspension bridges, and the celebrated annual Baliem Valley Cultural Festival. Renowned for sweet highland yams, traditional earth-oven Bakar Batu feasts, and colorful woven noken bags, it offers one of Indonesia’s most extraordinary highland cultures.

name: Papua Barat Daya
description: Crowning the northwestern tip of New Guinea around the lively maritime hub of Sorong, Papua Barat Daya is the gateway to the world-famous Raja Ampat archipelago. Its 1,500 limestone karst islands, turquoise lagoons of Wayag and Piaynemo, and record-breaking coral reef biodiversity make it one of Earth’s premier marine wonders. Alongside vibrant reefs, the province’s Bird’s Head rainforests shelter colorful birds-of-paradise, historic coastal towns, and fresh spice-grilled seafood served along Sorong’s waterfront.
